rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As in 27:5, rejection of the Qur’an comes from disbelief in the Hereafter, not from any lack of clarity in the Book.
rows.anchor: though this Qur’ ān is absolutely clear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opponents are in severe conflict about the Hereafter because they recoil from its responsibilities and evade its reality.
rows.anchor: the real reason is that they are in a severe mental conflict regarding the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an exposes a progression: evading the Hereafter corrupts their thinking, then they shut their eyes to signs around them because those signs impose responsibility.
rows.anchor: unveiled the gradual progression of their malady

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier exegetes have become confused over the interpretation of these words.
rows.anchor: our exegetes have ended up in confusion in the interpretation of these words

rows.speaker: the disbelievers
rows.claim: They find it strange that they could be raised again after dying and decaying in the earth.
rows.anchor: very strange to be raised to life again

rows.speaker: the disbelievers
rows.claim: They say the Hereafter threat is old: their forefathers received the same warning, which never came and will never come.
rows.anchor: their forefathers too were similarly threatened. It neither came nor will it ever come

rows.speaker: the disbelievers
rows.claim: They infer that such warnings are recycled tales of the ancients with no connection to reality.
rows.anchor: they deduce that all these are tales of the ancients which are repeated in every age

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cure for their blindness is to travel and learn from earlier nations’ fate; preserved traces of punishment show the warning is real.
rows.anchor: learn a lesson from the fate of earlier nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fate of wrongdoers in this world points to a coming day when God’s perfect justice and complete mercy will manifest.
rows.anchor: justice and complete mercy manifest themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should fulfill his duty and not grieve at opponents’ harshness or stubbornness; their conduct is their own wretchedness.
rows.anchor: He should fulfil his obligation and then leave them to themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not fear opponents’ schemes against him and his companions, since God can defeat them and save the believers.
rows.anchor: None of their tricks can trick God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic verb raddafa can occur with or without the preposition li; it means that something follows another thing.
rows.anchor: Examples of both are found in classical Arabic

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers’ rejecting nations are warned of two punishments: a worldly punishment for denial and the punishment of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: this world which necessarily visits them if they deny these messengers

rows.speaker: earlier rejecting nations
rows.claim: They ask when the Hereafter punishment will arrive and challenge the messenger to bring the worldly punishment if the final punishment cannot be brought forward.
rows.anchor: asking about the time of this punishment of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about what they seek to hasten means the Day of Judgement punishment, while “a part” means the worldly punishment; denial can bring a sample of the final punishment.
rows.anchor: refer to punishment of the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿalā indicates that worldly punishment depends on the nation’s attitude; most of Muhammad’s nation accepted faith and avoided the worldly punishment earlier nations faced.
rows.anchor: this punishment hinges on the attitude of the nation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comment continues that earlier nations faced worldly punishment, from which Muhammad’s majority of believers was spared.
rows.anchor: punishment that visited earlier nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s respite is mercy that lets people mend their ways, but they mistake it for proof that the messenger is a hoax and earn wrath instead of mercy.
rows.anchor: The last verse expresses sorrow on the attitude of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement reassures the Prophet and warns opponents: God knows their concealed schemes and public declarations and will deal with every mischief, reinforcing 27:70.
rows.anchor: These words sound assurance to the Prophet (sws) and warning to his opponents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse threatens the Prophet’s rivals: all secrets of heaven and earth are recorded openly with God, who will take account of everything.
rows.anchor: The last part of the verse is a threat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference is principally in response to Quraysh but also concerns Jews, who first stayed silent, then secretly supported Quraysh and were mentioned increasingly openly.
rows.anchor: This is in reference to the Jews though primarily

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an conveys truth to the Ishmaelites and explains disputed matters to Israelites; accepting it guides them to the straight path and brings mercy in this life and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: it is also explaining many facts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the Jews reject the Qur’an’s guidance, God will settle their disputes by His decisive final verdict; contextual indications identify this as the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: final verdict after which no one will be able to say anything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Yūnus gives a parallel: Israelites differed after receiving knowledge, and God will decide their disputed matters on Judgement Day.
rows.anchor: your Lord will decide the matters

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Hūd parallels this account: after Moses received the Book, people disputed it; a prior decree delayed their settlement and they remained in confounding doubt.
rows.anchor: Had a matter not been decided earlier by your Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah combines interpolated and conflicting narratives, making it impossible to distinguish truth from alteration; Jews were left in darkness, and they tried to extinguish the Qur’an’s offered light.
rows.anchor: an amalgam of conflicting narratives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s Qur’an sought to lead the Jews from darkness into light, but they tried to put out that light.
rows.anchor: they tried to put it out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should trust God’s support: he is on the truth that will prevail, and neither Quraysh nor Jewish rivals can succeed through their schemes.
rows.anchor: He should trust His Lord’s support

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet cannot make people hear when they are dead to the message or deaf and fleeing, but those who do not turn away and listen intently can understand.
rows.anchor: if they do not turn away and intently listen

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ʿan shows that hādī means turning the blind away from error and leading them to guidance; the Prophet cannot do this for them.
rows.anchor: blind from their error and lead them to guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb meaning “believe” expresses intention: only those who want to believe in God’s revelations can hear the call; those who seek to understand will accept faith and obey.
rows.anchor: expresses intention. Examples of this usage

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives everyone an urge to seek guidance; those who value it are guided further, while those who neglect it lose further guidance and their natural desire for guidance.
rows.anchor: those who duly value this urge are guided further by Him

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus is reported as explaining that what a person already has can be taken away from them.
rows.anchor: Even what they have is taken away from them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the word is fulfilled means that God’s verdict in this matter is declared and what the people deserve under His established practice becomes manifest.
rows.anchor: mean that when the verdict of God will be declared in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun them refers to Quraysh, who demanded that they would not believe in punishment or the Hereafter until they saw these or observed a sign; the demand appeared earlier in 27:71–73.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh who are addressed in this sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word used for the creature’s address does not mean ordinary speech here; it means bearing witness or presenting a sign, as in 30:35.
rows.anchor: to bear witness or present a sign in favour of something

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is giving them respite now to repent through the messenger and Book; after truth has been conclusively conveyed and they become liable to punishment, an animal from the earth will testify to their refusal of God’s revelations and deserving wrath.
rows.anchor: giving them respite to repent and mend their ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The animal’s testimony will follow when God decides to consign Quraysh to destruction, bearing evidence that they refuse His revelations.
rows.anchor: to consign them to destruction would be made

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The she-camel given to Thamūd through Ṣāliḥ is a parallel sign: he warned that harming it would bring wrath, and their harm to it was followed by punishment.
rows.anchor: he nominated a she-camel as such a sign

rows.speaker: our exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes describe the creature as a strange animal that will appear near Judgement Day.
rows.anchor: strange animal while explaining this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects applying the later strange-animal reports to this verse, arguing that they concern signs of Judgement Day and should be critically assessed.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this does not relate to this verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat to Quraysh was conditional: most eventually accepted faith and avoided a decisive punishment like that of ʿĀd and Thamūd, though wrongdoers among them died in battles with believers.
rows.anchor: gradually their majority accepted faith
